title: Onions: What Understanding Actually Means
author: Dylan Wiliam
summary: Wiliam uses a 5-by-5 magic square puzzle to expose what teachers mean by understanding, arguing that it is not a single thing but a nested series of claims teachers treat as equivalent at their peril. A pupil who can solve the puzzle once understands something; one who can explain why it works understands more; one who can prove and redesign it from first principles has peeled another layer. Assessment questions that probe only surface procedure mask the gap between fluency and genuine grasp, while questions that probe deeper layers (why does this work? what would change if...?) reveal what students actually know. Wiliam closes with the implication that understanding any concept has hidden layers, making humility about our own models and willingness to read closely and be wrong in public the core teacher moves.
points: Understanding is not a single achievement; it is a nested series of claims (solve it, explain why, prove it, generalise it) that surface-level assessment routinely conflates.
The question 'Do you understand?' is useless to a pupil because teacher and pupil can answer it honestly while meaning completely different things.

The deepest implication for teachers is humility: our own understanding has layers we have never surfaced, and discovering them requires reading closely, talking with peers, and being willing to be wrong in public.
quotes: What do we mean when we say a pupil “understands” something? The word is doing an astonishing amount of work in classrooms, and most of the time we don’t notice that it is.

Take five numbers, any five numbers. Arrange them in a 5×5 grid following a simple rule. Every row, every column, and both diagonals will sum to five times the middle number. That’s the trick. But what does it mean to “understand” it?

A pupil who can follow the procedure and produce the grid understands something. A pupil who can explain why every row, column, and diagonal sums to five times the centre understands something more.” “A pupil who can prove it, generalise it to n×n, and design a related puzzle from scratch has peeled another layer. These are not the same achievement, but we call them all “understanding.
The classroom consequence is that “Do you understand?” is a near-useless question, because teacher and pupil can answer it honestly while meaning completely different things.

The questions we ask, in the moment and on assessments, are what actually anchor our claim about what a pupil knows. A fluent procedure can hide an absent explanation; an absent explanation will trip them up later.

The most humbling moment in any teacher’s career is discovering that something you thought you understood has a layer you had never noticed. Good teaching is, in part, building habits that make that discovery routine rather than rare.

Understanding, like an onion, has layers. Our job is to know which layer we are asking about, which layer we are teaching to, and which layer our pupils are actually operating in.” Archived from Dylan Wiliam on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
